title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Pediatric postcardiac arrest syndrome remains a major contributor to morbidity and mortality despite return of spontaneous circulation. Mortality remains high due to a combination of recurrent cardiac arrest, hemodynamic instability, myocardial dysfunction, systemic ischemia–reperfusion injury, and secondary hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. Cardiac arrest in children most commonly arises from noncardiac etiologies, including respiratory failure, shock, sepsis, arrhythmias, electrolyte abnormalities, and severe acidosis. Following resuscitation, affected children frequently demonstrate hypotension, impaired tissue perfusion, altered mental status, and evolving multiorgan dysfunction. Effective postresuscitation care requires rapid identification of ongoing physiologic derangements and prompt initiation of targeted supportive therapies to stabilize cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic function.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity equips clinicians with advanced knowledge and practical skills for the systematic evaluation and management of pediatric patients after return of spontaneous circulation. Participants learn to perform structured postresuscitation assessments, optimize oxygenation and ventilation, manage hypotension and myocardial dysfunction with vasoactive support, and implement neuroprotective strategies, including targeted temperature management. Emphasis is placed on continuous monitoring, early recognition of complications, and identification of the underlying cause of arrest to prevent recurrence. The activity highlights the importance of coordinated interprofessional collaboration among critical care clinicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, pharmacists, and neurologic specialists. Effective communication within this team-based framework supports timely intervention, reduces secondary injury, and improves survival and neurologic outcomes.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Assess pediatric patients for clinical and diagnostic features of postcardiac arrest syndrome, including hemodynamic instability, neurologic impairment, and laboratory derangements. Develop protocols for continuous, multiparameter monitoring in pediatric patients with postcardiac arrest syndrome to enable early detection of physiologic disturbances and guide timely interventions. Apply evidence-based approaches to deliver personalized postresuscitation care, thereby minimizing complications and improving survival. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team, including specialists such as pediatric intensivists, neurologists, and rehabilitation physicians, to provide efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated care. title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Introduction
content: More than 20,000 pediatric cardiac arrests occur annually in the United States (US). [1] [2] [3] In the pediatric population, cardiac arrest typically results from progressive respiratory compromise or shock, with nonshockable rhythms such as asystole or pulseless electrical activity occurring more frequently than primary arrhythmias. [4] Mortality following pediatric cardiac arrest and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) remains greater than 90%. [5] ROSC is defined as restoration of sustained perfusion, achieved either through an effective native cardiac rhythm or extracorporeal support using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Initiation of ECMO during ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is termed "extracorporeal CPR" (ECPR). Improving outcomes after pediatric resuscitation requires addressing key elements of postarrest management to limit secondary organ injury.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Introduction
content: Resuscitation from cardiac arrest is commonly followed by the development of postcardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS), which may progress over days to weeks after sustained circulation is achieved. This syndrome comprises hypoxic–ischemic brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, a systemic ischemia–reperfusion response, and ongoing effects of the inciting pathology. Pediatric postcardiac arrest management emphasizes early anticipation, recognition, and treatment of this complex physiologic state to improve survival and neurologic outcomes. [6]

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Introduction -- Epidemiology
content: The timing and severity of PCAS phases may differ between out-of-hospital (OHCA) and in-hospital (IHCA) cardiac arrest. [7] An estimated 5000 children experience OHCA annually in the US, whereas approximately 6000 infants and children develop IHCA each year. [8] [9] [10] [11] After initial resuscitation from OHCA and admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (ICU), many children die during the postcardiac arrest period prior to discharge. [12]

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Introduction -- Epidemiology
content: Despite improvements in rates of ROSC and overall survival following pediatric cardiac arrest, PCAS affects more than 6000 children annually in the US. The primary objective of pediatric postcardiac arrest care (PCAC) is to improve survival to hospital discharge and optimize survival with favorable neurological outcomes. [13] [14] [15] Data collected from 2005 to 2013 indicate overall survival rates ranging from 6.4% to 10.2%. [16] Despite updates to postresuscitation management recommendations, survival to hospital discharge after OHCA has not changed significantly over the past decade. Most children who survive cardiac arrest sustain short- and long-term neurologic morbidities.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Phases of Postcardiac Arrest Syndrome
content: PCAS management requires multisystem support throughout each phase (see Image . Postcardiac Arrest Care Phases). The goals of care during all phases focus on limiting ongoing injury.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Overview of Postcardiac Arrest Management
content: During the post-cardiac arrest period, the healthcare team must anticipate and assess evolving systemic and organ dysfunction and proactively support organ function. Aggressive supportive care should be applied during this phase to maintain systemic perfusion and organ function. Goal-directed therapy represents a central component of pediatric PCAC, with multimodal targeting of key physiologic domains, particularly hemodynamic stability and adequate oxygenation and ventilation, likely providing greater benefit than isolated interventions. Pediatric cardiac arrest is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Factors linked to more favorable outcomes include in-hospital arrest, shorter arrest duration, prompt initiation of CPR, and hypothermia as the precipitating cause.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Therapeutic Hypothermia and Targeted Temperature Management
content: The 2019 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Pediatric Consensus on Science and Treatment Recommendations summarized evidence supporting the use of TTM, maintaining body temperature between 32 °C and 34 °C, after IHCA or OHCA in infants, children, and adolescents younger than 18. [18] [19] Continuous monitoring of core body temperature is required throughout TTM. In comatose infants and children aged 24 hours to 18 years following OHCA or IHCA, temperature may be managed with an initial hypothermic TTM phase at 32 °C to 34 °C, followed by controlled normothermia at 36 °C to 37.5 °C, or with normothermic TTM alone at 36 °C to 37.5 °C. Optimal TTM duration remains undefined. In the Therapeutic Hypothermia After Pediatric Cardiac Arrest trials, strategies included 48 hours at 32 °C to 34 °C followed by 72 hours at 36 °C to 37.5 °C, or a continuous 5-day period of TTM maintained at 36 °C to 37.5 °C. [20]

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Therapeutic Hypothermia and Targeted Temperature Management
content: Adequate analgesia and sedation are essential to maintain comfort and suppress shivering and may be supported with neuromuscular blockade when necessary. Opioids and benzodiazepines are commonly employed for effective pain control and sedation. Rewarming should be performed incrementally at approximately 0.25 °C to 0.5 °C/h to reduce the risk of hyperthermia. [21] Elevated body temperature during PCAC requires active management, as temperatures of 38 °C or greater are associated with higher mortality. Excessive cooling below 32 °C should be avoided to minimize the risk of adverse neurologic outcomes.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Hemodynamic Optimization
content: Hemodynamic support represents a cornerstone of PCAC, as inadequate perfusion strongly correlates with poor outcomes. Recommended approaches to vasoactive therapy and circulatory stabilization are described below.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Blood pressure
content: Hemodynamic instability after ROSC is common in children. Hypotension, defined as systolic blood pressure below the fifth percentile, after pediatric cardiac arrest, is associated with lower survival to hospital discharge. [22] [23] Fluid boluses and vasoactive agents should be administered according to guidelines.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Blood pressure
content: No pediatric interventional studies have evaluated the effect of manipulating blood pressure on survival after ROSC. However, poor perfusion is consistently associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as evidenced by both anecdotal observations and data analyses. Therefore, vasoactive therapy is recommended and should be tailored to each patient. No specific blood pressure target has been established, and vasopressors may need to be adjusted to optimize perfusion while avoiding excessive myocardial workload.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Circulatory support
content: Epinephrine infusion is the preferred agent for postarrest hypotension in pediatric patients. Early administration, within 15 minutes of OHCA, correlates with higher survival and improved neurological outcomes in children with nontraumatic, nonshockable cardiac arrest. [24] Epinephrine increases blood pressure through peripheral vasoconstriction and exerts inotropic and chronotropic effects. Other vasoactive agents, including dopamine, norepinephrine, and dobutamine, may support blood pressure but are generally reserved as second-line therapies or used selectively in specific conditions, such as renal failure or cardiogenic shock.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Oxygenation and Ventilation
content: Oxygenation and ventilation status represent essential components of postarrest assessment. Following ROSC, targeting a normal partial pressure of arterial oxygen is reasonable, with oxygen goals individualized for underlying conditions such as cyanotic congenital heart disease. The fraction of inspired oxygen should be maintained at the lowest level necessary to achieve an oxygen saturation between 94% and 99%. Hypoxemia should be avoided in PCAC, particularly during periods of oxygen adjustment. Oxygenation status should be monitored using continuous cardiac monitoring, continuous pulse oximetry, end-tidal carbon dioxide measurements, and intermittent arterial blood gases every 10 to 15 minutes to guide oxygen titration and support mechanical ventilation.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Oxygenation and Ventilation
content: Post-ROSC ventilation strategies should aim for normocapnia, defined as a partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) appropriate for the child’s physiology, typically 35 to 45 mm Hg, or a target tailored to underlying conditions. Prolonged periods of significant hypercapnia or hypocapnia should be avoided. Although the relationship between PaCO2 and partial pressure of end-tidal carbon dioxide (PetCO2) can support noninvasive monitoring, PetCO2 should be interpreted with caution, as variations in cardiac output and increased alveolar dead space may weaken the correlation with arterial values.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Arrhythmia
content: Rhythm disturbances observed during the postcardiac arrest period include premature atrial and ventricular contractions, supraventricular tachycardias, and ventricular tachycardias. Evidence is insufficient to support routine prophylactic administration of antiarrhythmics after ROSC. [25] [26] Persistent arrhythmias following ROSC should be managed pharmacologically according to the underlying cardiac anatomy and myocardial function. Consultation with pediatric cardiac electrophysiology specialists is often required. Many vasoactive agents used to support myocardial function can increase myocardial irritability and the risk of arrhythmias.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
content: Mechanical circulatory support with ECMO may be considered during PCAC when significant cardiorespiratory instability persists despite appropriate medical management. If ECMO is initiated during CPR (ECPR), support is typically continued into the postcardiac arrest phase until safe and reliable weaning from mechanical support is possible. The 2015 American Heart Association guidelines recommend consideration of ECPR for pediatric patients with IHCA and an underlying cardiac diagnosis. Overall, the clinical effectiveness of ECMO after ROSC remains inconclusive. Studies indicate ECMO may improve survival for rewarming and circulatory support in cold-water drowning victims.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Neurological Monitoring and Seizure Management After Return of Spontaneous Circulation
content: Serial neurological examinations can identify evolving hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. Due to the high incidence of subclinical seizures post-ROSC, monitoring with an electroencephalogram (EEG) supports therapy guidance and detection of evolving injury. [27] Neuroimaging can assist in identifying primary cerebral etiologies of cardiac arrest and in assessing the extent of severe brain injury.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Neurological Monitoring and Seizure Management After Return of Spontaneous Circulation
content: Brain computed tomography can identify treatable intracranial causes of cardiac arrest but has limited utility for predicting neurological prognosis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed after ROSC, together with serial neurological examinations, EEG, and adjunctive assessments, may help characterize neurological injury and potential recovery. Acute seizures detected on EEG are treated with benzodiazepines, levetiracetam, or phenytoin. Some seizures may be refractory to treatment.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Function -- Glucose Management
content: No interventional clinical trials of glucose control have focused exclusively on children during PCAC. Both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia are associated with unfavorable outcomes in children and adults with critical illness. [28] [29] [30] During the postresuscitation period, clinicians should promptly identify, prevent, and treat hypoglycemia (≤45 mg/dL in the newborn and ≤60 mg/dL in the child) to avoid further neurologic insult. Severe hyperglycemia can exacerbate postcardiac arrest volume depletion and hemodynamic instability.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Clinical Significance
content: The Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines have been revised repeatedly to improve survival after cardiac arrest. The most recent update was published in 2018. [31]

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Clinical Significance -- Prognosis
content: Favorable outcomes after cardiac arrest are more commonly associated with shorter arrest duration, prompt initiation of CPR, hypothermia as the precipitating cause, and arrests occurring in-hospital. Factors associated with unfavorable neurologic outcomes following OHCA include younger age, sudden infant death syndrome, and blunt trauma. Factors linked to decreased survival after IHCA include older age, preexisting conditions, interventions such as tracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor use at the time of arrest, as well as arrests occurring during night or weekend shifts. In both OHCA and IHCA, prearrest rhythms of bradycardia, ventricular fibrillation, or tachycardia are associated with the highest survival, while pulseless electrical activity shows higher survival than asystole.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Clinical Significance -- Prognosis
content: Beyond the initial reperfusion phase, several factors may compromise cerebral oxygen delivery and contribute to secondary brain injury in the hours to days following cardiac arrest. These factors include hypotension, hypoxemia, impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation, and brain edema. Hyperglycemia is common after cardiac arrest and correlates with poor neurological outcomes following OHCA.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PCAC is typically initiated in the emergency department and continues in the ICU for children who achieve survival. This phase of care is resource-intensive and requires coordination among a broad interprofessional team, including intensivists, neurologists, primary care clinicians, ICU nursing staff, social workers, ethics consultants, organ donation services, and spiritual care providers. Child protective services may also be involved in selected cases.

title: Pediatric Postresuscitation Management -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Given the high mortality associated with cardiac arrest and the substantial risk of poor neurological outcomes among survivors, early and transparent communication with families is essential. Early involvement of ethics teams and bereavement support services is recommended. Survivors of pediatric cardiac arrest frequently sustain hypoxic-ischemic brain injury with long-term impairments in daily functioning, highlighting the importance of comprehensive discussions regarding potential outcomes. Regular updates and continuous communication from the clinical team support family understanding of the clinical trajectory and preparation for possible outcomes. An interprofessional care model is critical, as postcardiac arrest management places substantial demands on healthcare resources and contributes to provider stress while presenting emotional challenges for families and care teams. Coordinated and integrated responses from care providers across prehospital, emergency department, and ICU settings may improve outcomes for initial survivors.
